findings.text: The first paragraph tells a newcomer what Athena is, who it is for and what problem it solves, in plain words. From it alone they could explain Athena to someone else.
findings.source: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. ... It solves the problem of AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable."

findings.text: A next step is linked near the top, and the Next steps section is concrete: it gives the repo, the clone command, prerequisites, `./setup.sh`, and a sample `athena ask "add a changelog"`. The newcomer knows what to do next.
findings.source: "Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself" (header) and the "Next steps" section

findings.text: This is the Athena site, but its title and almost all of its body are about a different project, firstmate. A newcomer may at first think firstmate is the product. The second paragraph clears this up, but only after the title has set the wrong idea.
findings.source: Title: "Athena explains how firstmate handles work"

findings.text: The headline promise is a request that becomes a commit, with cost and verdict recorded. The page never shows that: there is no example request, cost or verdict. The study shows a different skill (reading a codebase), so the main pitch is never demonstrated.
findings.source: "get back a commit they can trace to the request, the models, the cost and the verdict"

findings.text: This header link is for the site's owner, not a visitor. A newcomer won't know whose decisions it means or whether it concerns them.
findings.source: "Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision."

findings.text: Most of the page is detailed firstmate internals: exit codes, guards, 12 transition cards and 45 claims. It shows how rigorous the study is, but a newcomer who came to learn about Athena will likely skim or leave. "Start here" helps by giving a short path through it.
findings.source: Sections "Transitions" and "Claims and sources" (e.g. "If every place of a declared capacity is held, the spawn exits 75")

findings.text: The page says Athena is written in Rust, but the prerequisites don't mention a Rust toolchain or say whether setup.sh installs one. They also don't say whether running a request needs an account or costs money.
findings.source: "Before installing, have git 2.40 or later, a C linker, curl, and either Claude Code or npm"

findings.text: Every claim carries a "mechanism" or "prose-only" tag, but the glossary doesn't define either one. A reader has to guess that "prose-only" means the rule is only an instruction and no code enforces it.
findings.source: Claims list tags "mechanism" and "prose-only"; Glossary entry "mark"

findings.text: The page openly states its limits: nothing was run, and the first reading missed several paths. This supports the page's own claim that every statement is traced to a source. Some newcomers may also read it as a sign the tool is unreliable.
findings.source: "A first reading of the pinned tree missed these paths" (Limits of this study, f3)

findings.text: This note refers to a `studies/` folder without saying which repository it is in, so a newcomer can't act on it.
findings.source: "This page's study id, firstmate-work-handling, is the name of the folder under studies/" (About this page)
